title: Sincere repentance
hook: turn to Allah in sincere repentance (66:8)

segments.voice: Yesterday: a way out, the exit promised in the middle of the divorce rules. Your line was a way out comes. Did you look at a corner of a problem you'd been ignoring? Day six hundred thirty-four.

There's the fake apology. "I'm sorry you feel that way." "Mistakes were made." The sorry that's mostly about getting the conversation over with. And there's the other kind, rarer, the one where you can hear that the person has actually stopped, looked at what they did, and turned around. Surah sixty-six, at-Tahrim, has a name for that second kind. It asks the believers for a repentance that is, in its word, nasuh.

Verse eight, in Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Turn unto Allah in sincere repentance!" The Arabic is tawbatan nasuha. Tawbah, repentance, comes from a root that means to return, to come back. It's not mainly about feeling bad. It's about turning around and walking home. And one of the names of Allah comes from the same root: at-Tawwab, the One who turns, again and again, toward the one who turns back. So both sides are moving. Nasuh is the hard part. It shares a root with nasihah, sincere advice, the kind a true friend gives. A nasuh repentance has nothing hidden in it, no deal on the side, no plan to do it again on Friday. Scholars such as Imam an-Nawawi set out what that looks like. You stop the wrong thing. You regret it. You resolve not to return to it. And if it hurt another person, there's a fourth step: you make it right with them, return what was taken, ask their pardon. A hadith in Ibn Majah puts the heart of it in a few words: regret is repentance. And this verse doesn't come with a scolding. It comes with a hope: perhaps your Lord will remit your bad deeds. Not perhaps you'll earn it. Perhaps He will. One more thing: sincere doesn't mean perfect. In the scholarly tradition, someone who truly repents and later slips hasn't made the first repentance fake. They turn back again. The door the verse describes doesn't lock after the first use.

The practice: repent of one thing, meaning it. Sit, and let one thing come up. Not your whole life. One thing, maybe small, a sharp word, a corner cut. Walk it through the four steps, quietly. Can I stop? Do I regret it? Will I not go back? Is there someone I owe a repair? Don't argue with yourself. Just let the answers come. If you pray, this is a moment for astaghfirullah, I seek Allah's forgiveness. If you don't, simply turn toward the better thing. The bell holds the time.
Sincere repentance. Tawbatan nasuha, a turning back with nothing hidden in it: stop, regret, resolve, and repair what you broke. Today's word.
Your line: turn back sincerely. If you owe someone an apology today, give the real kind: name what you did, without "but," and offer to make it right. Day six hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Muslims repent (tawbah) by stopping a wrong, regretting it and resolving not to return to it, and, when another person was harmed, by making amends; astaghfirullah, I seek Allah's forgiveness, is a familiar phrase of daily speech.

fork.setup: you wronged a friend and you're truly sorry before Allah. by the scholars' steps, is regret enough?
options: no, you also make it right with your friend.
fork.reveal: when a wrong touched another person, scholars like an-Nawawi add a fourth step: repair it with them, or ask their pardon.

original.note: Arabic: a sincere repentance (66:8). tawbah, a turning back; nasuh, pure of any hidden motive.

trapdoor: what you thought: saying sorry to God.
what it means: turning back with nothing hidden: stop, regret, resolve, and repair what you harmed.
what a scholar hears: tawbah and at-Tawwab share the root t-w-b, to return; nasuh shares n-s-h with nasihah, sincere counsel.
